title: Professional Bread Scoring Tips for a Perfectly Open Crumb
keyword: how to get better oven spring sourdough
meta_description: Master the art of bread scoring and boost oven spring for sourdough. Learn expert tips, tools, and techniques to achieve a perfect open crumb every bake.
html:
When you’re chasing that airy, open crumb, the secret often lies in how you shape and score the loaf. Understanding how to get better oven spring sourdough starts with a confident hand and the right tools. A clean, decisive slash lets steam escape at the right moment, giving the dough the lift it needs while creating the classic decorative pattern you see in bakery windows. Below are the practical steps that have helped me turn a stubborn, flat loaf into a beautifully risen masterpiece.

1. Master the Basics of Dough Development

Before you even think about the lame, the dough must be strong enough to hold a cut without tearing. This begins with proper hydration, bulk fermentation, and fold techniques. Aim for a hydration level around 70‑75% for most sourdoughs; higher hydration yields a more open crumb but requires more handling skill. During bulk fermentation, perform a series of stretch‑and‑folds every 30 minutes until the dough shows glossy, elastic windows. These folds develop gluten, which is the structural network that enables a good oven spring.

2. Timing the Score for Maximum Oven Spring

The moment you score the loaf is critical. If you score too early, the dough will deflate; too late, and the crust will set before the expansion can occur. The sweet spot is when the dough has risen about 70‑80% of its final volume and the surface feels slightly tacky but not dry. This usually coincides with the “poking test” – gently press a finger into the dough; the indentation should slowly spring back without bouncing.

3. Choosing the Right Scoring Tool

While a sharp kitchen knife works in a pinch, a dedicated bread scoring lame offers better control and a cleaner cut. The 3‑in‑1 Sourdough Whisk Set includes a professional‑grade lame with a razor‑thin blade that glides through the dough without dragging. The same set also provides a Danish dough whisk for efficient mixing and a dough scraper for handling sticky doughs—both essential for keeping the surface smooth before scoring.

4. Scoring Techniques That Encourage Open Crumb

Here are three reliable patterns that promote strong oven spring and an attractive crumb:

  1. Single diagonal slash: Position the lame at a 45‑degree angle and pull the blade toward you in one swift motion. This creates a single, deep cut that releases steam efficiently.
  2. Cross‑plus: Make a short diagonal cut, then rotate the loaf 90° and add a second cut intersecting the first. The intersecting lines create two expansion points, encouraging the loaf to rise evenly.
  3. Leaf pattern: Use a series of shallow, parallel slashes (about ¼‑½ inch apart) followed by a deeper central cut. The shallow cuts guide the expansion, while the deep cut provides the main steam release.

Whichever pattern you choose, keep the blade angled and pull confidently. A hesitant cut can crush the dough surface and reduce oven spring.

5. Steam Management in the Oven

Even the best score won’t shine without proper steam. Preheat a cast‑iron Dutch oven or a baking stone, then add a pan of boiling water or a spray bottle of water just after loading the loaf. The steam keeps the crust supple for the first 10‑12 minutes, allowing the scored cuts to open fully. After that, remove the steam source to let the crust firm up and develop a golden‑brown color.

6. Post‑Bake Care for an Open Crumb

Once the loaf is out of the oven, cool it on a wire rack for at least an hour. This cooling period lets the crumb set and prevents the interior from becoming gummy. Slice the loaf with a serrated bread knife, not a straight blade, to preserve the airy structure you worked so hard to create.

FAQ

What is the ideal blade angle for scoring?

A 45‑degree angle gives the best balance between depth and control. It allows the cut to open quickly while minimizing tearing.

Can I use a regular kitchen knife instead of a lame?

You can, but a lame’s ultra‑sharp, thin blade produces cleaner cuts and reduces drag, which directly improves oven spring and crumb openness.

How often should I replace the lame blade?

When the blade begins to dull or shows visible nicks, replace it. A dull blade will crush the dough surface, diminishing the lift.
